from pypdf import PdfReader

reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import re
from pathlib import Path
from statistics import mean
rows=[]
for line in Path('tmp/pdfs/page-13.txt').read_text().splitlines():
    match=re.match(r'"'^'"\\s*([a-z][a-z ]+?)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)',line)
    if match:
        rows.append((match[1].strip(),*[float(match[i]) for i in range(2,6)]))
print('Table 11 occupation rows:',len(rows))
print('Means single SS, %F, paired SS, %F:',[round(mean(r[j] for r in rows),4) for j in range(1,5)])
print('Means male-associated rows:',[round(mean(r[j] for r in rows[:20]),4) for j in range(1,5)])
print('Means female-associated rows:',[round(mean(r[j] for r in rows[20:]),4) for j in range(1,5)])
power=[]
for line in Path('tmp/pdfs/page-15.txt').read_text().splitlines():
    match=re.match(r'"'^'"\\s*([a-z][a-z ]+?)\\s+(minor|power)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)',line)
    if match:
        power.append((match[1].strip(),match[2],*[float(match[i]) for i in range(3,6)]))
print('Table 13 power rows:',len(power))
for category in ['minor','power',None]:
    group=[r for r in power if category is None or r[1]==category]
    print('Means',category,[round(mean(r[j] for r in group),4) for j in range(2,5)])
print('Figure 4 occupational mean individual adherence implied by both=71.9%,any=74.3%:',(71.9+74.3)/2)
print('Figure 4 power mean individual adherence implied by both=57.9%,any=59.7%:',(57.9+59.7)/2)
PY"

strengths: PST addresses a meaningful question for multimodal NLP: whether gender associations change when two social roles are depicted together. The occupational and organizational-power settings give the evaluation practical relevance.

The reported results support increased conventional stereotype alignment under paired prompts: occupational SS rises from 10.00 to 47.38, and organizational-power SS from 4.62 to 18.98. These are substantial descriptive differences.

Three human annotators assess each target individual, with reported Fleiss’ kappa scores of 0.88–0.92. Testing and reporting BLIP’s poor agreement on paired images strengthens the justification for human annotation.
Explicit prompt templates, descriptor lists, both positional orders, and detailed per-occupation tables make the evaluation design understandable and support reconstruction of the prompt inventory.
weaknesses: The central fairness interpretation is not established. Section 3.1 defines fairness as gender parity for each attribute, but SS measures signed stereotype alignment. In Table 2, single-person scores of +50 and −30 cancel to an overall 10; an always-feminine generator would score zero across balanced stereotype groups. Low aggregate SS therefore does not establish fair single-person generation, and an increase does not by itself establish greater overall unfairness. This distinction materially affects the central claim.

Figure 4 compares events with different baselines. Independent gender-balanced pairs would contain at least one stereotype-conforming individual 75% of the time, so the headline that over 74% of generations demonstrate bias is not independently diagnostic. The high PST(Both) frequency is more informative, but the analysis needs calibrated baselines and explicit joint gender distributions.

The single-person baseline uses only three images per identity. This cannot reliably establish occupation-specific fairness or anti-stereotypical tendencies, particularly when examples are selected for large observed differences. Confidence intervals and statistical tests are absent. More baseline samples, matched organizational-role compositions, and uncertainty estimates are needed to substantiate the amplification analyses.

Annotation agreement does not verify that generated people actually satisfy the requested roles and positions. No systematic prompt-fidelity assessment or DALL-E 3 failure rate is reported. The organizational-power template specifies the occupation only for the first subject, leaving the shared-industry interpretation ambiguous. Appendix C also permits 'Cannot Identify' responses without explaining their treatment in the binary metric or label aggregation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. Exact sampled organizational-role pairs, generation settings, access dates/interface, and handling of any prompt rewriting are unspecified; code and data are only promised upon acceptance. Section 3.2.2 also states 944 total prompts while describing 800 occupational plus 1,152 power prompts. The prompt inventory, executed samples, and retained annotations should be reconciled.

The mitigation conclusions exceed the evidence from one intervention on one effectively evaluated model. Selecting the most biased occupations and regenerating them requires a fresh untreated comparison to assess selection effects. The organizational-power score changing from 18.98 to −11.12 needs uncertainty estimates before establishing reverse bias and does not demonstrate general failure of prompt-based mitigation. These measurement, comparison, and reproducibility issues require revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
